beats.narration_text: Hola, this is Liam, in for Bear. This is how Walker is meant to be asked: hand it a game design document, get back a playable Godot project. The prompt on screen is a reconstruction, not a transcript, because this game was rebuilt first, and its document came after.

props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about a 2.5D brawler-platformer — a night shift in a container yard, three Y Bots to choose from, ledges, wall jumps, an axe and a hammer, and a Forewoman at the end — into a playable Godot project.
props.runningText: illustrative reconstruction — not the historical prompt
output: What happened: a Unity platformer with no levels was rebuilt in Godot first.
GDD.md was written afterwards, from the evidence.

beats.narration_text: Night Yard came before its design document. Unity left a hundred and fifty scripts and a yard full of art, but no scenes, no levels and no sound. The rebuild made all six levels. The document was written last, and nothing in it is signed off.

props.text:
Night Yard
was built from its GDD.
Nothing is signed off.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant writer: text is typed on screen over the narration, so mid-beat samples legitimately show a partial page. The finished six-line text fills the safe area and holds for the last 1.5 s.

beats.narration_text: The document separates six kinds of claim: recovered from the Unity code, invented for the rebuild, built, observed, proposed, or still waiting on a person. Built: seventeen scripts, five thousand lines. Observed: the game's own playtest passes, and seventy-eight assertions pass in this film's three scripted takes. Human playtests: zero.

beats.narration_text: The vision is a proposal: a night shift in a container yard. Climb the stacks, fight past the yard bots, take down the Forewoman. Who it's for is left open. The pillars are read off the code: move like a stuntman, fight with what you have, and read the yard.

beats.narration_text: Here's the core loop on the real build, played by a script, not a person. The banner. A yard light is ten points. A bot knocked out is ten more. At a hundred the gate opens, the player walks through, and the panel shows the time.

beats.narration_text: Four experience goals, all proposed, each with a test a person has to run. The captures can only hint. The script never fell in level one's pit by accident, because it knows the map. And it was knocked out five times by the Forewoman before it won. Whether that feels fair is a person's call.

beats.narration_text: Movement follows Unity's controller: walk, run, a running turn, a double tap that runs. The rebuild measured the walking clip's stride, one point six five metres a second, and runs at five point two. One catch: the double tap is timed on the wall clock, not game time.

beats.narration_text: Jumping is tuned to the grid. A jump peaks at about two point one metres, so a two metre step can be jumped onto, and a three or four metre wall needs the ledge grab. A running jump clears a three wide gap. Holding into a wall while falling slows the fall, and jump kicks off it.

beats.narration_text: Combat ports Unity's attack system. Sixteen attacks, each with its own clip window and the hands, feet or blade that must actually touch. Three presses chain jab, cross and kick. The hammer does nine damage to a bot, can't be blocked, and recharges in nine seconds.

beats.narration_text: The rules are Unity's numbers: a hundred HP, ten points a light, a hundred to win. A K.O., a spike plate or a fall sends you back to the last checkpoint. The plate fires point four seconds after something steps on it, and kills whoever is still standing there.

beats.narration_text: The bots run Unity's AI: path over the level's links, jump or drop, attack in range, re-roll the attack every two seconds. New: they start unaware, which is what makes a takedown possible. The Forewoman has twelve HP, blocks often, and swings the hammer too.

beats.narration_text: Unity delivered no levels. All six are new, each built around one move: the first ledge, the wall jump shaft, the axe, the slide tunnel and the takedown, the hammer against a crowd of fourteen, and the boss. They're text maps on a one metre grid.

beats.narration_text: The world is authored: a yard at night on a side-view grid, with the industrial pack behind the lane, placed from a seed. Blocks between the camera and the player fade out. The three characters share every clip through Godot's humanoid retargeting. And the sound is new: the Unity export had none.

beats.narration_text: Under the hood, one class runs every fighter, the player and every bot, with the same eight input flags. The player's come from the keyboard; a bot's come from its brain. Out of scope, by decision: Unity's editor tools and demo code.

beats.narration_text: The game's own test plays every level, but it wires the bot brain straight into the player. The captures keep the player on the keyboard: the same brain decides, and its decisions become key presses. Five questions remain for a person, including whether the boss is fair.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. This document organizes; it doesn't approve. The loop runs end to end on real key presses, through six levels, the Forewoman and the credits, and through the failures. The rebuild's own levels are labelled. One defect slipped past the game's own test. What's left is a person's call: the audience, the story, and whether the boss is fair.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude with your own design document: Here is my game's design document. Pick one proposed experience goal. Rewrite it as a hypothesis with a test I can run with three players, and tell me which result would make me change the design. If no result would change your mind, it isn't a hypothesis yet. Liam, in for Bear.
